subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Breast cancer: risk factors and histologic types
vignette: A 60-year-old woman presents with a hard, irregular breast mass in the upper outer quadrant. The mass is fixed to the pectoral muscle and overlying skin, producing nipple retraction and skin dimpling.
question: Which of the following best explains the skin and nipple changes?

options.text: Dermal lymphatic invasion by tumor cells
Invasive carcinoma fixed to Cooper ligaments and pectoral fascia
Mammary duct ectasia with subareolar fibrosis
Fat necrosis with a calcified oil cyst
Paget disease with intraepithelial adenocarcinoma

explanation_correct: Breast cancer is commonly postmenopausal and often presents as a palpable hard mass, most often in the upper outer quadrant. Invasive cancer can become fixed to the pectoral muscles, deep fascia, Cooper ligaments, and overlying skin, producing nipple retraction and skin dimpling. Most breast cancers arise from the terminal duct lobular unit, and invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common type, forming a rock-hard mass with desmoplastic stroma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Dermal lymphatic invasion produces inflammatory carcinoma with warm, swollen, erythematous peau d'orange skin and usually no palpable mass, not a fixed hard mass with dimpling.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mammary duct ectasia is a benign fibrotic dilation of subareolar ducts causing discharge and nipple inversion, not a hard fixed mass with skin dimpling.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fat necrosis is a benign painless lump with a calcified oil cyst after injury, not a fixed malignant mass with nipple retraction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Paget disease presents with eczematous patches on the nipple and areola with Paget cells (intraepithelial adenocarcinoma), not a deep fixed mass with dimpling.

educationalObjective: Invasive breast cancer (usually ductal) is a hard upper-outer-quadrant mass that fixes to Cooper ligaments/skin causing nipple retraction and dimpling.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Breast cancer: risk factors and histologic types
vignette: A medical student is reviewing breast cancer risk factors. She wants to identify which of the following patients has the highest risk of developing breast cancer.
question: Which of the following is most strongly associated with an increased risk of breast cancer in females?

options.text: Early age at first pregnancy and a history of breastfeeding
Low cumulative estrogen exposure, such as early menopause and high parity
Black race as the group at highest overall risk
Increasing age, atypical hyperplasia, a BRCA mutation, and nulliparity
A history of fibrocystic changes with simple cysts

explanation_correct: Major female breast cancer risk factors include increasing age, history of atypical hyperplasia, family history, BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations, increased estrogen exposure (eg, nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause), postmenopausal obesity (adipose tissue converts androstenedione to estrone), more menstrual cycles, absence of breastfeeding, later age at first pregnancy, and alcohol intake. White patients have the highest overall risk, while Black patients have a higher risk of triple-negative breast cancer. In males, BRCA2 mutations and Klinefelter syndrome increase risk.

explanation_incorrect.A: An early first pregnancy and breastfeeding are protective factors, lowering breast cancer risk rather than raising it.
explanation_incorrect.B: Low cumulative estrogen exposure (early menopause, high parity) is protective; high estrogen exposure is the risk factor.
explanation_incorrect.C: White patients have the highest overall risk of breast cancer; Black patients have a higher risk specifically of triple-negative tumors, not the highest overall risk.
explanation_incorrect.E: Nonproliferative fibrocystic changes such as simple cysts do not increase cancer risk.

educationalObjective: Breast cancer risk is increased by age, atypical hyperplasia, BRCA mutations, nulliparity, postmenopausal obesity, and alcohol; White women have highest overall risk, Black women higher triple-negative risk.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Breast cancer: risk factors and histologic types
vignette: A 48-year-old woman has an invasive breast cancer. Immunohistochemistry shows tumor cells that are negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2. Her oncologist notes this subtype tends to be more aggressive.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this tumor?

options.text: Triple-negative breast cancer, which is more aggressive
HER2-positive breast cancer, which has amplification of an EGF receptor
ER-positive breast cancer that responds well to hormonal therapy
Luminal A carcinoma with the most favorable prognosis
A noninvasive carcinoma confined to the ductal lumen

explanation_correct: Amplification/overexpression of estrogen and progesterone receptors or HER2 (an EGF receptor) is common in breast cancer. Triple-negative tumors (ER-negative, PR-negative, HER2-negative) lack all three and form a more aggressive subtype with fewer targeted therapy options. The patient's immunoprofile is therefore triple-negative breast cancer.

explanation_incorrect.B: HER2-positive tumors overexpress HER2 (an EGF receptor); this tumor is HER2-negative by immunohistochemistry.
explanation_incorrect.C: ER-positive tumors express estrogen receptor and may respond to hormonal therapy; this tumor is ER-negative.
explanation_incorrect.D: Luminal A tumors are ER/PR-positive and generally have a favorable prognosis, unlike this receptor-negative tumor.
explanation_incorrect.E: A noninvasive carcinoma confined to the ductal lumen would be DCIS, not an invasive cancer with this receptor profile.

educationalObjective: Triple-negative (ER-/PR-/HER2-) breast cancers are more aggressive; ER/PR/HER2 amplification is common in other subtypes.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Breast cancer: risk factors and histologic types
vignette: A 56-year-old woman is diagnosed with early-stage invasive breast cancer. Her oncologist is discussing the single most important prognostic factor in early-stage disease.
question: Which of the following findings is the most important prognostic factor in early-stage breast cancer?

options.text: Expression of estrogen receptors
Tumor location in the upper outer quadrant
Axillary lymph node metastasis
Presence of microcalcifications on mammography
Patient age over 50

explanation_correct: In early-stage breast cancer, axillary lymph node metastasis is the single most important prognostic factor. The presence and number of involved nodes guide staging and therapy. Other features such as receptor status and tumor location matter, but nodal involvement is the key prognostic determinant in early disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Estrogen receptor status guides therapy and has prognostic value, but it is not the most important prognostic factor in early-stage disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tumor location (upper outer quadrant) is a typical presentation site but is not a prognostic factor.
explanation_incorrect.D: Microcalcifications are a mammographic clue (eg, DCIS) and are not the principal prognostic factor.
explanation_incorrect.E: Age is a risk factor for developing breast cancer, but it is not the most important prognostic factor in early-stage disease.

educationalObjective: Axillary lymph node metastasis is the most important prognostic factor in early-stage breast cancer.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Breast cancer: risk factors and histologic types
vignette: A 50-year-old woman has a routine mammogram that shows clustered microcalcifications. No palpable mass is felt. Biopsy shows neoplastic ductal cells filling the ductal lumen with an intact basement membrane.
question: Which of the following best describes this lesion?

options.text: Invasive ductal carcinoma with desmoplastic stroma
Lobular carcinoma in situ with loss of E-cadherin
Paget disease of the nipple
Inflammatory carcinoma with dermal lymphatic invasion
Ductal carcinoma in situ, an early malignancy without basement membrane penetration

explanation_correct: DCIS fills the ductal lumen with neoplastic cells but is an early malignancy that has not penetrated the basement membrane. It often appears early as microcalcifications on mammography and usually does not produce a palpable mass. It arises from ductal atypia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Invasive ductal carcinoma penetrates the basement membrane and produces a rock-hard mass with desmoplastic stroma, unlike this in-situ lesion with an intact basement membrane.
explanation_incorrect.B: LCIS shows loss of E-cadherin and is an incidental finding without mass or calcifications, rather than ductal microcalcifications.
explanation_incorrect.C: Paget disease extends up lactiferous ducts into the nipple skin causing eczematous patches, not an asymptomatic mammographic microcalcification finding.
explanation_incorrect.D: Inflammatory carcinoma involves dermal lymphatic invasion with a warm, swollen, erythematous breast and poor prognosis, typically without a mass, not an in-situ ductal lesion.

educationalObjective: DCIS fills ductal lumens with neoplastic cells, appears as microcalcifications without a mass, and has not invaded through the basement membrane.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Breast cancer: risk factors and histologic types
vignette: A 58-year-old woman presents with a persistent eczematous, scaly patch over the nipple and areola that has not responded to topical treatments. Biopsy of the skin shows large pale cells within the epidermis. Mammography reveals an underlying DCIS.
question: Which of the following best explains the nipple skin findings?

options.text: Extension of an underlying DCIS or invasive cancer up the lactiferous ducts into the nipple skin (Paget disease)
A superficial fungal infection of the nipple
Mammary duct ectasia with subareolar fibrosis
Fat necrosis with a calcified oil cyst
Nonproliferative fibrocystic change

explanation_correct: Paget disease results from extension of an underlying DCIS or invasive breast cancer up the lactiferous ducts and into the contiguous skin of the nipple and areola, producing eczematous patches. The Paget cells are intraepithelial adenocarcinoma cells (large pale cells within the epidermis). An underlying DCIS or invasive cancer is typically present.

explanation_incorrect.B: A superficial fungal infection would not contain intraepithelial adenocarcinoma cells, nor would it be associated with an underlying DCIS on mammography.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mammary duct ectasia is a benign fibrotic dilation of subareolar ducts in smokers with multicolored discharge and nipple inversion, not eczematous skin with Paget cells.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fat necrosis is a benign lump with a calcified oil cyst and giant cells after injury, not an eczematous nipple with malignant cells.
explanation_incorrect.E: Nonproliferative fibrocystic change causes cyclical bilateral lumps and cysts, not an eczematous nipple patch with intraepithelial adenocarcinoma.

educationalObjective: Paget disease is eczematous nipple/areolar skin from underlying DCIS or invasive cancer extending up lactiferous ducts, with Paget cells (intraepithelial adenocarcinoma).

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Breast cancer: risk factors and histologic types
vignette: A 46-year-old woman has an incidental breast biopsy performed for another indication. It shows a proliferation of loosely cohesive cells with loss of E-cadherin expression within the lobules, with no mass or calcifications identified.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this lesion and its implications?

options.text: DCIS, which increases risk in the same breast and quadrant
Invasive ductal carcinoma with desmoplastic stroma
Paget disease with eczematous nipple changes
LCIS, which increases cancer risk in either breast
Fibroadenoma with no increased risk

explanation_correct: LCIS shows decreased E-cadherin expression and produces no mass or calcifications, so it is typically an incidental biopsy finding. Unlike DCIS (which increases risk in the same breast and quadrant), LCIS increases the risk of invasive carcinoma in either breast. Similarly, invasive lobular carcinoma shows loss of E-cadherin with single-file cells and is often bilateral. The loss of E-cadherin and lack of a mass or calcifications point to LCIS.

explanation_incorrect.A: DCIS fills ductal lumens, is associated with microcalcifications, and raises cancer risk in the same breast and quadrant, not an incidental lobular proliferation with E-cadherin loss.
explanation_incorrect.B: Invasive ductal carcinoma forms a rock-hard mass with desmoplastic stroma and small glandular cells, not an incidental in-situ lobular lesion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Paget disease involves eczematous nipple skin with Paget cells from an underlying malignancy, not an asymptomatic lobular proliferation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fibroadenoma is a small mobile fibroglandular mass in younger women with no increased cancer risk, not an E-cadherin-deficient lobular lesion.

educationalObjective: LCIS has decreased E-cadherin, no mass or calcifications (incidental), and raises cancer risk in either breast, unlike DCIS (same breast/quadrant).

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Breast cancer: risk factors and histologic types
vignette: A 52-year-old woman presents with a warm, swollen, erythematous breast with skin thickening around hair follicles giving a peau d'orange appearance. She has breast pain but no discrete palpable mass. She was initially treated for mastitis without improvement.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Lactational mastitis
Mammary duct ectasia
Inflammatory breast carcinoma
Paget disease of the nipple
Fat necrosis

explanation_correct: Inflammatory carcinoma results from dermal lymphatic space invasion by tumor, producing breast pain with warm, swollen, erythematous skin around exaggerated hair follicles (peau d'orange). It usually lacks a palpable mass and carries a poor prognosis (about 50% survival at 5 years). It is often mistaken for mastitis or Paget disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Lactational mastitis occurs in breastfeeding women with nipple cracks and S. aureus infection; it would not show peau d'orange or dermal lymphatic invasion, and this patient is not described as breastfeeding.
explanation_incorrect.B: Mammary duct ectasia is a benign smoking-associated condition with multicolored discharge and nipple inversion, not a warm swollen peau d'orange breast.
explanation_incorrect.D: Paget disease produces eczematous patches on the nipple/areola with Paget cells, not diffuse warm swollen skin with peau d'orange.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fat necrosis is a benign painless lump with a calcified oil cyst after injury, not an erythematous swollen breast with dermal lymphatic invasion.

educationalObjective: Inflammatory breast carcinoma is dermal lymphatic invasion causing a warm, swollen, peau d'orange breast, often without a palpable mass, with poor prognosis and frequently mistaken for mastitis.
